meaning.evidence: Every point is kept, with added asides: "(more than once! the old goat)", "empty as a pub at sunrise", "read and read and read till the cows come home". These hang off the original, though "Fair dinkum." and "Stuck fast." are padding.

sense.evidence: Terms mostly fit: "noggin", "chockers", "a ripper of a time". "downed tools on our former works in parallelopipeds" strains a little in the mock-formal report, but carries "abandoned".

authenticity.evidence: Some lines are natural ("I haven't let on to anybody, mind", "what she's on about"), but stock phrases are bolted on: "Fair dinkum.", "till the cows come home", "empty as a pub at sunrise", "a dead important one".

register.evidence: The brief is level 2, but the slang is heavy: "noggin", "salt-and-pepper job", "Fair dinkum.", "ripper", "chockers", "Hooroo", "Chrissie", "the old goat". Closer to level 3-4. No swearing, as asked.

tone.evidence: Judy's chirpy, teasing voice mostly survives ("Oh, you see, I know!"), but the pub-flavoured additions ("empty as a pub at sunrise", "the old goat") roughen a schoolgirl's letter.

flow.evidence: Readable, with pile-ups: "a sort of sprinkly grey, salt-and-pepper job, or maybe nothing up there at all" and "Stuck fast." after "I _am_ stuck".

variety.evidence: Wide range of slang with little repetition: "noggin", "chockers", "ripper", "Hooroo", "See ya", "on the go", "snuck off".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the letter, its question and its reading list, but the additions push it towards a yarn: "the old goat", "Fair dinkum."

problems.why: Stock Aussie tag bolted onto the end of a paragraph; nothing in the original calls for it.

A.summary: Lively and full of meaning, but overdone for a level-2 brief, with stock phrases bolted on.

meaning.evidence: Essentially the original word for word, so everything survives: "You never answered my question and it was very important."

sense.evidence: The few swaps mostly fit ("verandah roof", "heaps of others"), but "I’m going to have a beautiful time in holiday" renders "in vacation" ungrammatically.

authenticity.evidence: What little Aussie there is ("beaut red bath robe", "merry Chrissie!") sits next to untouched US forms: "Good-by, Daddy", "Good-by till January--and a merry Chrissie!", "a beautiful time in holiday".

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: apart from spelling ("colour", "realising") and "verandah", "heaps", "beaut", "Chrissie", it is the original. Lighter than level 2.

tone.evidence: The original's voice is intact because the text is: "Oh, you see, I know! You’re a snappy old thing with a temper."

flow.evidence: Reads as the original, except the broken join "a beautiful time in holiday" and the mismatched "Good-by till January--and a merry Chrissie!"

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original, since it barely changes: "ARE YOU BALD?"

B.summary: Faithful because barely touched; a few swaps, one of them ungrammatical.

meaning.evidence: Everything is there, closely tracked: "I've got you worked out exactly--very satisfactorily, too--", "bought it with $1.12 of last month's allowance".

sense.evidence: Each term fits: "four on the go at once", "what she's on about", "Hooroo, Daddy", "a beaut time over the holidays".

authenticity.evidence: Natural, unforced Australian: "If you can't be bothered writing", "The corridors are that cluttered", "cos there are eighteen blank years behind me". "my beaut red bath robe" is slightly odd.

register.evidence: A light, steady touch, right for level 2: "cos", "beaut", "Turns out", "Hooroo", "See ya in January--and a merry Chrissie!". No swearing.

tone.evidence: Judy's bright, teasing voice comes through: "Oh, you see, I know! You're a snappy old thing with a temper on you." The mock-formal Saturday report stays mock-formal.

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly aloud: "I've got a new rule, and it's unbreakable: never, ever study at night".

variety.evidence: Varied, though "beaut" appears twice ("beaut red bath robe", "a beaut time").

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the letter, retold lightly: "But here's the problem: shall I add some hair?"

problems.why: 'Beaut' as attributive for a bathrobe is a touch forced, and it is repeated later in 'a beaut time'.

C.summary: Light, natural and faithful; exactly the weight of a level-2 brief.

meaning.evidence: All points survive: "there's another Freshman from Texas staying back too", "(that _would_ mark me as a bit odd)". "and pretty well, too" softens "very satisfactorily" slightly.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "chock-a-block", "staying back", "dressing-gown", "crabby old thing". "left by the wayside" for "getting left out" is a fair fit.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian English: "hop into my nice red dressing-gown", "The corridors are so chock-a-block", "Hooroo, Daddy". Nothing stagey.

register.evidence: Light, maybe a shade lighter than level 2: "chock-a-block", "Hooroo", "on the go", but it ends "Bye till January--and a merry Christmas!"

tone.evidence: The voice is kept: "Oh, you see, I know! You're a crabby old thing with a temper on you." "crabby" loses a little of the fond "snappy".

flow.evidence: Mostly smooth, but "a sort of sprinkly grey sort of hair" repeats "sort of", and "I've got it all worked out exactly what you look like" is a clumsy join.

variety.evidence: Varied but sparse: "chock-a-block", "staying back", "Hooroo", "on the go", "on about".

D.summary: Natural and faithful, slightly light on Aussie, with a couple of clumsy joins.

meaning.evidence: Mostly complete, but some details are flattened: "very satisfactorily" is dropped ("I've got you all worked out--down to a tee--"), "a properly assorted family" becomes "a proper family", and "studying is getting left out" becomes "nobody's doing any study".

sense.evidence: Terms fit well: "last month's pocket money" for allowance, "first-year" for Freshman, "chockers", "let on". "at uni" for college fits Australian usage.

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "I haven't let on to anybody", "The stuff most girls ... just soak up", "If you can't be bothered writing".

register.evidence: Right weight for level 2: "cos", "chockers", "beaut", "Hooroo", "See ya", "Chrissie", with no swearing.

tone.evidence: Judy's voice is warm and teasing: "You're a cranky old thing with a temper, I reckon."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "I've got a new rule, and there's no breaking it: never, ever study at night".

variety.evidence: Varied: "down to a tee", "mates", "chockers", "pocket money", "first-year", "uni", "Hooroo", "See ya".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the letter, with a little flattening of its period wit: "a proper family" for "a properly assorted family".
